answer.headline: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
answer.text: It happens in chloroplasts, in two linked stages: the light-dependent reactions capture energy, and the Calvin cycle uses that energy to build sugar.
points: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green
The oxygen released comes from splitting water, not from carbon dioxide

items.title: Light is absorbed
items.text: Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light and excites electrons.

items.title: Water is split
items.text: Replacing those electrons splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen gas.

items.title: Energy carriers are made
items.text: The electron flow produces **ATP** and **NADPH**, the short-term energy carriers.

items.title: Carbon is fixed
items.text: In the stroma, the enzyme **RuBisCO** attaches CO₂ to a five-carbon sugar (the Calvin cycle).

items.title: Sugar is built
items.text: ATP and NADPH turn the fixed carbon into a three-carbon sugar, used to make glucose, starch and sucrose.

items.v: Chloroplasts, mostly in leaf mesophyll cells

items.title: Light intensity
items.text: More light speeds the reaction until another factor limits it.

items.title: Carbon dioxide
items.text: Often limiting in bright light; greenhouses sometimes add CO₂.

items.title: Temperature
items.text: Enzymes work faster when warmer, but too much heat slows or stops them.

blocks.label: Common exam mistake
blocks.body: Plants **also respire**, day and night. Photosynthesis does not replace respiration; in light, photosynthesis is usually faster, so there is a net release of oxygen.

items.a: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly and reflects much of the green, so green light reaches our eyes.

items.q: Does the Calvin cycle need light?
items.a: Not directly, which is why it was once called the 'dark reactions'. It does depend on ATP and NADPH from the light stage, so in practice it slows down in the dark.

items.q: Where does the plant's mass come from?
items.a: Mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, fixed into sugars. Water and soil minerals contribute much less of the dry mass.

blocks.text: Light energy in, chemical energy out: photosynthesis stores sunlight in the bonds of sugar.
